stories.title: Genentech Tops Out $2B Holly Springs Manufacturing Facility
stories.excerpt: Genentech raised the final beam of its new manufacturing facility in Holly Springs, North Carolina, during a topping-out ceremony. The milestone reflects continued progress on Genentech’s approximately $2 billion investment in its first-ever East Coast manufacturing facility. The project, announced in May of 2025, broke ground in August of 2025. Completion is expected in 2029. Once operational, the 700,000-square-foot facility will produce next-generation treatments for metabolic conditions, such as obesity. It will incorporate advanced biomanufacturing, automation, robotics and the latest digital manufacturing technologies designed to increase production efficiency, support sustainability, and strengthen Genentech’s U.S.-based supply chain. The project is expected to support more than 2,000 jobs, including more than 500 high-wage manufacturing roles and more than 1,500 construction jobs. The facility is part of Roche and Genentech’s broader $50 billion commitment to R&D and manufacturing infrastructure in the U.S. Roche and Genentech’s current U.S. footprint includes 13 manufacturing sites, 15 research and development sites and approximately 25,000 employees across 24 locations in eight states. The post Genentech Tops Out $2B Holly Springs Manufacturing Facility appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Genentech topping out $2B Holly Springs, NC biomanufacturing facility; completion 2029.
Project will create 2,000+ jobs including 500 high-wage manufacturing roles.
Part of Roche/Genentech's $50B U.S. R&D and manufacturing infrastructure commitment.
stories.summary: Genentech reached topping-out on its first East Coast biomanufacturing facility in Holly Springs, North Carolina—a $2 billion investment announced in May 2025 and broken ground in August. The 700,000-square-foot facility will produce next-generation obesity treatments using advanced automation and robotics, and is expected to complete in 2029. The project will support more than 2,000 jobs, including over 500 high-wage manufacturing positions, and is part of a broader $50 billion capital commitment by Roche and Genentech to strengthen U.S.-based infrastructure across 24 locations in eight states.
stories.impact: Major employer investment signals sustained job growth and in-migration to Holly Springs and the Raleigh-Durham region through 2029 completion and beyond. The 2,000+ jobs—especially 500 high-wage manufacturing roles—will drive demand for workforce housing in surrounding submarkets; developers should begin acquiring and underwriting multifamily sites within 10-15 miles of the facility now to capture leasing velocity when operations begin. This is a rare, multi-year visibility window for demand in a secondary market.

stories.title: Shifting Fortunes for L.A.’s Ports Boost Surrounding Industrial Real Estate
stories.excerpt: Ports are meant to offer protection from storms or rough seas. But nothing has been able to protect the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach from the uncertainty and fluctuation of trade policy during President Donald Trump’s second term. “It’s like the quote from ‘The Morning Show,’” said Gregg Healy, executive vice president and head of Savills Industrial Services. “Chaos is the new cocaine. I do think we will have more turbulent times ahead.” So it’s been a welcome surprise that the tariff turbulence has seemed to benefit industrial real estate near or tied to the waterfront. From Liberation Day in April 2025, when Trump announced his first round of sweeping tariffs, to the current war with Iran, the ebbs and flows of global trade have been massive and disruptive, but new shipping volume is helping port-adjacent and port-dependent submarkets. Amid a boom and bust cycle that’s dominated the last few years, and pushing warehouse vacancy to a recent peak of 7 percent this year, Los Angeles’ industrial side may be poised for an upswing. People watch as a container ship departs from the Port of Los Angeles. PHOTO: Mario Tama/Getty Images Shipping volume at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach is up 1.8 percent this year. After topping 1 million container units in June, the Port of Los Angeles nearly hit that mark in July, making it the second-busiest July on record. “Businesses continue to move cargo when they see windows of opportunity amid an evolving trade environment, while resilient consumer demand is helping keep imports at historically strong levels,” said Port of Los Angeles Executive Director Gene Seroka in a recent statement. The region’s industrial market saw its highest leasing levels in five years during the second quarter of 2026, according to Cushman & Wakefield data, driven by its centrality to larger logistics networks. bullets: L.A./Long Beach port volatility and tariff turbulence benefiting port-adjacent industrial real estate.
Shipping volume surges offsetting boom-bust cycles; Los Angeles industrial warehouse vacancy peaked 7% in 2025.
Trade policy uncertainty creating strong demand for port-dependent warehouse and logistics space.
stories.summary: Despite tariff chaos and trade policy uncertainty since April 2025's "Liberation Day," industrial real estate near the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach has benefited from new shipping volume and port-dependent tenant demand. Los Angeles industrial vacancy recently peaked at 7 percent this year as the market cycles through boom-and-bust conditions tied to global trade flows. Port-adjacent and port-dependent submarkets are now poised for an upswing, with shipping volatility paradoxically driving increased logistics demand.
stories.impact: Port turbulence and rising shipping volume are fueling near-term industrial demand in L.A. County, but this is a logistics/industrial signal, not multifamily. However, logistics job concentration near the ports (truck drivers, warehouse workers, port staff) creates demand for affordable, transit-accessible multifamily in Long Beach, Carson, and other port-adjacent working-class submarkets—developers should monitor ramp-ups in logistics hiring and port worker wage trends to underpin lease-up assumptions in these corridors.

stories.title: West Palm Beach Developer Buys Lot, Apartments on Way
stories.excerpt: Estate Cos. bought a lot in West Palm Beach and plans to build the second phase of a two-phase apartment project. The S. Floirda Business Journal reports the company paid $13 million for a 1.19-acre lot at 411 West Railroad. The seller was Sunview Cos. Banesco USA provided an $8.45 million mortgage to the buyer. For the first phase, the 321-unit, eight-story Soleste Palm Station, just west of this site, is still under construction. For Phase II, The Estate Cos. plans to develop the new site with 310 apartments in 15 stories. For Soleste Palm Station Two, the multifamily community will include 411 parking spaces and a pool deck. Estate Companies says it identifies and coordinates investment opportunities for both private and institutional investors. It’s focus, since 2012, is on high-yielding, risk-adjusted, development and investment opportunities (land and residential projects) in the South Florida region. bullets: Estate Cos. bought 1.19-acre lot in West Palm Beach for $13M; phases II and I total 631 units.
Phase II: 310 apartments in 15 stories; Phase I (Soleste Palm Station) 321 units, 8 stories.

stories.summary: Estate Cos. purchased a 1.19-acre lot at 411 West Railroad in West Palm Beach for $13 million to develop Phase II of a two-phase apartment project. Phase I, the 321-unit eight-story Soleste Palm Station, is currently under construction. Phase II will add 310 apartments across 15 stories with 411 parking spaces and a pool deck. Banesco USA financed the acquisition with an $8.45 million construction loan.
stories.impact: West Palm Beach submarket showing strong multifamily development velocity—two consecutive phases by same developer signal confident underwriting and off-plan absorption; Phase I success is de-risking Phase II lease-up. Comparable South Florida markets (Boca Raton, Delray Beach) are likely seeing similar phase-based builds. Monitor Phase I pre-leasing, rents, and traffic for signals on submarket absorption pace and whether South Florida as a whole is still capturing in-migration strength.

stories.title: McDowell Starts Work on Hudson Age-Restricted, Affordable Apartments
stories.excerpt: McDowell Housing Partners closed on a construction loan and started work on Ekos at Bayonet Point II, the second phase of a three-phase master-planned community that will bring 360 affordable homes to Pasco County. The $38.9 million development will add 120 age-restricted apartments at 7526 McDowell Way in Hudson, one block from HCA Florida Bayonet Point Hospital. Rents and incomes will be restricted across three tiers of Area Median Income (AMI). The development was financed with tax-exempt bonds issued by Florida Housing Finance Corporation (FHFC), 4% housing tax credits, and subordinate financing awarded by FHFC through its SAIL, ELI and HOME-ARP programs. Wells Fargo Community Lending & Investment provided equity through the purchase of the housing tax credits and placed the senior construction financing. Permanent financing will be provided by Freddie Mac and serviced by Wells Fargo Multifamily Capital. Amenities include a standalone clubhouse with a pool and covered patio, a fitness center, a computer lab, a game and crafts area, and a dog park. Ekos at Bayonet Point II is expected to be complete in spring 2028. The post McDowell Starts Work on Hudson Age-Restricted, Affordable Apartments appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: McDowell Housing Partners closed $38.9M construction loan; Phase II of 120 age-restricted apartments in Hudson, FL.
Financed via tax-exempt bonds, 4% housing tax credits, SAIL/ELI/HOME-ARP; Freddie Mac permanent financing.
Completion spring 2028; one block from HCA Florida Bayonet Point Hospital; rents restricted across three AMI tiers.
stories.summary: McDowell Housing Partners closed a $38.9 million construction loan and began work on Ekos at Bayonet Point II, Phase II of a three-phase affordable master-planned community in Pasco County. The 120-unit, age-restricted development in Hudson will feature rent and income restrictions across three AMI tiers and is financed via Florida Housing Finance Corporation's tax-exempt bonds, 4% housing tax credits, and state HOME-ARP programs. Wells Fargo provided equity and senior construction financing; Freddie Mac will provide permanent financing. Expected completion is spring 2028.
stories.impact: Pasco County affordable, age-restricted supply is being absorbed via permanent debt and tax-credit equity; strong feasibility signals that baby-boomer workforce and seniors relocating to Tampa Bay region are generating sustainable demand. Proximity to HCA hospital adds employer stability. Monitor whether broader Pasco County (Wesley Chapel, New Tampa) is seeing similar age-restricted pipeline—this could signal underserved demographic wave and identify adjacency opportunities for market-rate seniors or caregiver workforce housing.

stories.title: Retail Landlords Need to Underwrite Their Tenants’ Customer Base, Too
stories.excerpt: Landlords underwrite the retail tenant. But they almost never underwrite the tenant’s customer. They should. That gap costs landlords money, and it is fixable before a listing goes live. The standard leasing process is too reactive: Review comparable rents, post the space on Crexi and LoopNet, wait for responses, and then vet an operator’s finances. Mark Kvetkovskiy. None of that tells you whether enough of that retailer’s customers live near the space. If they do not, the risk rises of tenant failure, months of vacancy, and another round of commissions and negotiations. The better approach is to flip the process. Instead of waiting to see who shows up, start by studying who lives near the space. How do nearby households spend? Which categories over-index locally? Does the neighborhood support an everyday concept, a destination brand, or something in between? Answer those questions first, and you can define the customer already walking the neighborhood’s streets. Then, identify the brands that serve that customer and approach them directly about the vacancy. Proactive outreach can reduce days on market and the vacancy costs that come with them. Consider a hypothetical vacant restaurant at Rivington and Ludlow streets on Manhattan’s Lower East Side. I analyzed the 2026 Esri Consumer Spending Survey and Esri Market Potential data for the area within a five-minute walk. Esri’s modeled data draws on consumer surveys, demographic segmentation and household spending patterns. It is directional, not a record of observed transactions. Esri estimates that households in that walking area spend $50,243,250 annually on food and beverages away from home, or about $5,043 per household. The market-potential data then sharpens the picture. Some 20.4 percent of adults in the area visited a fine-dining restaurant in the previous six months, an index of 124, or 24 percent above the U.S. average. bullets: Article advises retail landlords to underwrite tenant customer base, not just tenant financials.
Proactive outreach to tenant candidates based on neighborhood demographics reduces vacancy and commissions.
Gap in standard underwriting (comparable rents → listing → operator vetting) ignores local demand dynamics.
stories.summary: A retail leasing best-practices article argues that landlords should proactively analyze the customer demographics living near a space before listing it, rather than waiting for operator applications and then vetting the tenant's financials. By studying local household spending patterns, categories that over-index, and defining which brands align with the neighborhood, landlords can reduce vacancy and negotiate from a position of strength. The standard reactive process—posting comparable rents, listing on Crexi/LoopNet, and vetting operator finances—fails to validate whether the retailer's customer base actually exists locally.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development, but the principle applies: multifamily developers must validate resident demand profiles (income, lifecycle stage, employment, transit needs) before underwriting site locations and unit mixes. A weak article for this audience; brief mention only.

stories.title: Inflation Is Down. But Consumers Aren’t Out of the Woods Yet
stories.excerpt: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 3.4% year over year in July. Meanwhile, the core CPI, which excludes food and energy costs, rose 2.5%. Both measures fell slightly month over month. They also matched market expectations and suggested that inflationary pressures could be moderating. A recent Marcus & Millichap report supported that possibility, noting that despite continued turmoil in the Middle East and its potential impact on supply chains, the latest readings could “modestly ease immediate pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.” Rent Growth Continues Muted Housing remains one of the largest contributors to the core CPI, with the Owners’ Equivalent Rent (OER) accounting for much of the metric. Also counted are apartment rents. These increased by 1.3%, compared with the 2.1% increase the year before. At the same time, real average hourly earnings declined 0.1%. This suggests that consumers’ purchasing power remains under pressure even as inflation moderates. Consumer Spending Faces Headwinds Food prices continued to climb in July, with year-over-year grocery and restaurant prices increasing by 2.7% and 3.4%, respectively. “Although this divergence may suggest consumers remain willing to spend on discretionary dining, it may also signal vulnerability if household purchasing power weakens further,” Marcus & Millichap said. Retail property fundamentals were mixed. Vacancy remains 60 basis points below its historical average, as space demand remains volatile. Net space relinquishment occurred in three of the past six quarters. The report suggested that retailers are working in a resilient consumer environment but are selective about spending. Hospitality Could Feel the Pressure Leisure spending is under pressure, too. bullets: CPI 3.4% YoY July 2025; core CPI 2.5%; apartment rents +1.3% (down from +2.1% prior year).
Real average hourly earnings declined 0.1%; consumer purchasing power remains under pressure.
Housing (incl. OER and apartment rents) remains largest contributor to core CPI.
stories.summary: U.S. Consumer Price Index rose 3.4 percent year-over-year in July 2025, with core CPI at 2.5 percent—both matching expectations and suggesting inflation may be moderating. Apartment rents increased 1.3 percent compared to 2.1 percent the prior year, indicating rent growth is cooling. However, real average hourly earnings declined 0.1 percent, meaning consumers' purchasing power remains under pressure despite moderating inflation. Housing, including apartment rents and Owners' Equivalent Rent, continues to be the largest contributor to core CPI inflation.
stories.impact: Apartment rent growth decelerating (1.3% vs. 2.1% YoY) signals softer pricing power in rental markets; combined with declining real wages, resident rent-to-income ratios are tightening. Developers should lower rent growth assumptions in new underwritings and expect slower absorption in Class B/C markets where renters are most wage-sensitive. Markets with wage growth (tech hubs, high-skill job centers) will outperform those dependent on lower-wage service sectors.

stories.title: Retail Regains Its Footing as Demand Returns and Supply Stays Soft
stories.excerpt: After a soft first quarter, the retail sector regained positive momentum in Q2 as tenant demand returned, vacancies remained stable and new construction stayed limited. According to second-quarter reports from CBRE, Colliers, Cushman & Wakefield, JLL and Lee & Associates, the combination is creating a favorable setup for landlords and investors, even as retailers contend with increasingly selective consumers. Absorption Retail demand returned in the second quarter, reversing the Q1 negative absorption created, in part, by multiple move-outs. Ongoing tenant demand and the backfilling of vacant space in Q2 helped overcome that first-quarter softness. Some retail categories also benefited from back-to-school spending, with clothing, sporting goods and school supplies among the areas reporting sales growth. Construction New retail supply remained limited, with higher construction costs and continued financing challenges discouraging speculative development. Most new projects are concentrated in build-to-suit and grocery-anchored developments, where tenant demand provides greater certainty. Sunbelt markets continue to account for the lion’s share of construction activity. The supply constraints are helping support modest rent growth nationwide. Investment Investors remain actively interested in retail, with first-half 2026 sales volume reaching $33 billion, a 14% increase from the same period last year. Stronger sales momentum is putting pressure on pricing and contributing to cap-rate compression. Outlook Retail construction is expected to remain sluggish and concentrated in select Sunbelt metros, keeping vacancies low into 2027. Consumers are likely to remain value-conscious, benefiting discount retailers as well as specialty and off-price centers. Well-capitalized retailers and those with strong value propositions should remain better positioned to handle potential headwinds. bullets: Retail sector momentum returned in Q2 2025 after soft Q1; vacancies stable, new construction limited.
Tenant demand recovering; combination favorable for landlords despite selective consumer behavior.
CBRE, Colliers, Cushman & Wakefield, JLL, Lee & Associates all reporting positive Q2 metrics.
stories.summary: After a weak first quarter, the retail sector regained momentum in Q2 2025 as tenant demand returned, vacancies stabilized, and new construction remained limited. According to reports from major brokers (CBRE, Colliers, Cushman & Wakefield, JLL, Lee & Associates), the combination of recovering demand and constrained supply is creating favorable conditions for landlords and investors, even as retailers contend with increasingly selective consumer spending.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development, but signals broader CRE capital deployment may favor retail over residential in H2 2025, potentially tightening equity and debt availability for multifamily development in some markets. Monitor cap rate spreads between retail and multifamily to determine if retail repricing is happening and pulling capital away from residential.

stories.title: T&E Development Buys West Chelsea Site for $34M From PPHE Hotel Group
stories.excerpt: A development site in Manhattan’s West Chelsea area previously conceived for hotel and luxury residences in 2019 by an international hospitality firm is now poised for a new residential journey. Amsterdam-based PPHE Hotel Group sold the property at 538-542 West 29th Street to Brooklyn-based T&E Development for $33.5 million in a deal that closed late Thursday afternoon, Commercial Observer has learned. Colliers represented the seller with a team led by Zach Redding, Dylan Kane and Jared King. Sporn Group’s Lenny Sporn arranged the sale on behalf of the buyer. Crain’s New York Business first reported that the deal was set to close this summer. PPHE Hotel Group announced in March 2019 it had formed a joint venture with developer Largo to acquire the vacant lot for around $42 million, with plans to build a 98-key hotel and 55 condos. An entity connected to PPHE field demolition permits for the project in late 2023, Crain’s reported at the time. Greg Hegarty, co-CEO of PPHE, said in a February statement on the pending sale that “significant changes to the regulatory landscape” for ground-up development of hotel projects in New York following its 2019 acquisition contributed to the decision to part ways with the property. The 9,875-square-foot vacant lot between 10th and 11th avenues has 74,063 square feet of development potential under New York City’s C6-3 zoning within the Special West Chelsea District and will not require an affordable housing component, according to Colliers. T&E recently completed a 54-unit condo development called the Florian at 350 East 18th Street in Manhattan’s Gramercy Park. Redding said the property is one of the few remaining unconstrained development sites in West Chelsea and would be well positioned as a residential project given there is only one condo building currently under construction between West 20th and West 30th streets. bullets: T&E Development bought 538-542 West 29th St, Manhattan West Chelsea for $33.5M from PPHE Hotel Group.
Site originally planned as 98-key hotel + 55 condos in 2019; now pivoting to residential.
Property sale reflects shift from hospitality to residential in post-COVID Manhattan; PPHE abandoned hotel plans.
stories.summary: Brooklyn-based T&E Development acquired a development site at 538-542 West 29th Street in Manhattan's West Chelsea from Amsterdam-based PPHE Hotel Group for $33.5 million. PPHE had announced plans in March 2019 to build a 98-key hotel and 55 condos (as a joint venture with developer Largo), but the company shifted strategy and sold the vacant lot to T&E, signaling a pivot from hotel to residential development. The buyer's plans for the site were not disclosed.
stories.impact: Manhattan West Chelsea—a prime Hell's Kitchen/Hudson Yards-adjacent submarket—is showing continued conversion from hospitality to residential. The price paid (~$33.5M for a development site) and PPHE's retreat from hotel suggest continued weakness in NYC hotel underwriting post-2019, while residential remains investable. T&E likely planning market-rate apartments; monitor leasing velocity and rents once project is announced to gauge whether West Chelsea/Hudson Yards renters are stable post-remote-work transition.

stories.title: L.A. County Investment Sales Jump 28% in July Thanks to Multifamily
stories.excerpt: Commercial real estate investment sales accelerated across Los Angeles County in July, with multifamily accounting for the majority of capital deployed. About 7.25 million square feet of commercial property traded for $2.1 billion last month, NAI Capital reported Thursday, citing CoStar data. Compared to July 2025, almost 22 percent more square footage traded hands during July to make for a 28.5 percent jump in dollar volume. Compared with July 2024, sales volume climbed 75 percent. The gains came despite elevated borrowing costs, with long-term Treasury yields remaining near multiyear highs. Multifamily dominated, with 3.43 million square feet changing hands for $1.22 billion — accounting for 58 percent of all investment during the month in L.A. County. Sales volume increased 55 percent since last year, and almost 166 percent compared to July 2024. Average pricing rose 28.7 percent to $376 per square foot. People look at the Los Angeles skyline from Griffith Observatory. PHOTO: Matt McNulty - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images Retail also posted broad gains. About 1.23 million square feet sold for $402 million, pushing dollar volume up 40 percent from a year ago, and nearly doubling the July 2024 total. Retail square footage traded has climbed 135 percent over the same two-year period. Industrial faces a more complicated environment. About 1.33 million square feet traded in July, which is almost 71 percent higher since 2025, but dollar volume remained about flat at $214 million, and average pricing fell 3.6 percent to $273 per square foot. Office was the only major property type to decline in both sales volume and square footage. About 1.26 million square feet sold for $262 million, down 9.7 percent and 23.4 percent, respectively, from July 2025. Average pricing dropped 23.5 percent to $250 per square foot. bullets: L.A. County investment sales jumped 28.5% YoY in July 2025 ($2.1B, 7.25M sq ft); multifamily drove gains.
Multifamily: 3.43M sq ft, $1.22B (58% of county sales); volume +55% YoY, pricing $376/sq ft (+28.7% YoY).

stories.summary: Commercial real estate investment sales across Los Angeles County surged 28.5 percent in July 2025, reaching $2.1 billion for 7.25 million square feet, according to NAI Capital. Multifamily led the surge, with 3.43 million square feet trading for $1.22 billion—58 percent of all county investment volume. Multifamily sales volume climbed 55 percent year-over-year and 166 percent compared to July 2024, while average pricing rose 28.7 percent to $376 per square foot. Gains occurred despite elevated long-term Treasury yields near multiyear highs.
stories.impact: L.A. County multifamily experiencing strong investor demand and rising valuations (+28.7% pricing YoY) even with high rates—signals strong local demand fundamentals (in-migration, job growth, rent resilience) overriding cost-of-capital headwinds. Acquisition windows narrowing as comp pricing rises; developers should accelerate land optioning and site control in L.A. submarkets (Koreatown, Mid-City, Downtown, Westside infill) before pricing gaps close further. Investors repricing risk downward, suggesting cap rates may be tightening despite rate environment.

stories.title: New York City’s Technology Labor Market Has Surpassed San Francisco: Report
stories.excerpt: It’s official. New York is employing more tech workers than the San Francisco Bay area. According to an annual CBRE report on North American tech talent, the New York metropolitan area’s tech workforce reached 394,300 in 2025. The stat marks an 8.4 percent increase from 2022 that added 30,640 jobs. Meanwhile, San Francisco’s tech employment fell by 6 percent over the same period, totaling 375,730 jobs in 2025. This is the first time in the report’s 13-year history that the Big Apple has come out ahead. The city’s diversified job market helped set it apart, Colin Yasukochi, executive director of CBRE’s tech insights center, told Commercial Observer. “What really pushed New York past the San Francisco Bay Area has been the job reductions that we’ve seen [in San Francisco], with a lot of the announced layoffs, and the fact that New York has continued to grow,” Yasukochi said. San Francisco remains in North America’s top spot for its pool of tech talent, however, ranked across 13 metrics. The report, which analyzed the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and LinkedIn data, found that tech jobs make up more than 10 percent of total employment in San Francisco, compared to just 4.2 percent in New York. But a whopping 61 percent of San Francisco’s tech talent works directly in the tech industry, according to CBRE’s report, leaving its general labor market vulnerable. In New York City, just 34 percent of its tech workers work within the industry, while 21 percent work in tech roles in finance, insurance and real estate industries (otherwise known as FIRE). “[That] has given New York resilience from the tech downturn that broadly started in 2022, in terms of employment,” Yasukochi said. “But, obviously, with the artificial intelligence industry coming into play, that’s turned around quite substantially in the last year.” Yasukochi added that New York also benefits from a massive university infrastructure and lower wages than San Francisco, on average, for
bullets: NYC tech workforce 394,300 in 2025 (+8.4% since 2022, +30,640 jobs); exceeded San Francisco for first time.
San Francisco tech employment fell 6% over same period to 375,730 jobs; announced layoffs drove exodus.
NYC's diversified job market outpaced SF's concentration; first time in 13-year CBRE report history NYC leads.
stories.summary: New York City's technology labor market surpassed San Francisco's for the first time in 2025, with NYC's tech workforce reaching 394,300 (up 8.4 percent since 2022, adding 30,640 jobs). San Francisco's tech employment fell 6 percent over the same period, totaling 375,730 jobs. According to CBRE's annual North American tech talent report, NYC's diversified job market and continued growth outpaced San Francisco's tech concentration and announced layoffs. San Francisco remains ranked first in overall tech talent pool across 13 metrics.
stories.impact: NYC's tech employment overtaking San Francisco signals sustained in-migration of higher-wage tech workers to Manhattan and Brooklyn through at least 2025. This supports continued rent growth and Class A multifamily absorption in Manhattan (Midtown South, Flatiron, Williamsburg) and emerging Brooklyn corridors (DUMBO, Brooklyn Heights, Park Slope). Developers should model stronger absorption and rent assumptions in Manhattan submarkets competing for tech talent (finance, media tech, advertising) and prioritize transit-accessible sites near tech clusters (Hudson Yards, Flatiron, Tribeca). West Coast developers should monitor whether SF's tech job losses are stabilizing or accelerating, and whether Austin, Denver, Seattle are capturing displaced SF talent instead.
